purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and inspected-source provenance for P29–P34, completing the narrative movement family. Fields remain outside strict Commons frontmatter.

articles.title: Give the Scene a Want
use_when: A scene contains activity but no legible reason for events to matter to its participant.
The writer’s purpose for including the scene is clear but the person’s immediate concern is not.
A broad ambition never takes a local form the reader can follow.
goals: Room for quiet, changing, and contradictory desires
mechanisms: Distinguishing the writer’s narrative purpose from the participant’s local intention
Giving a broad desire a present expression through narration, action, or a request
Making uncertainty and competing concerns readable without imposing a complete goal-conflict-outcome formula
not_ideal_when: An observational, associative, or collective passage organizes attention effectively by another means.
A neat intention would overwrite uncertainty or the evidence available in factual narrative.
example_user_queries: Things happen in my scene, but it still feels directionless.
I know why I need the scene, but not what the character wants while they are there.
My protagonist has a big ambition but no immediate concern in this encounter.
How can I establish a scene’s purpose without announcing a mission?
Can I simply tell readers what someone wants?
Does a quiet scene need an opponent or an obstacle?
My character’s goal changes halfway through the scene.
How can two contradictory wants both remain believable?
Can a character want something unrelated to the main plot?
How do I write a real person’s intention when their reasons are uncertain?

sources.author: The Old Vic
sources.title: Writing a scene
sources.inspected_material: The written playwriting guidance on what the two participants want, why, and how their actions respond as the situation changes.
sources.supports: Considering a participant’s local want as a source of direction within a scene.
sources.limits: Only the written page was inspected, not the embedded video. Its exercise and examples are not reproduced. The article does not adopt mandatory opposition or tactics as a formula for every prose scene.

sources.inspected_material: The official page transcript on immediate objectives, underlying motivation, shifting goals, conflicting desires, and motivations beyond the story’s main pursuit.
sources.supports: Distinguishing local aims from deeper motivations and allowing multiple or competing concerns.
sources.limits: The article adopts no literary example, exercise, claim about film production history, clinical analogy, or sponsor claim. Tessa and Inez are original fiction. Quiet scenes, writer-versus-participant purpose, and nonfiction evidence are editorial development.

visual_decision.implementation: Self-contained prose examples make implication, speaker ownership, or local intention directly readable. A table or graphic would add little; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Make Resistance Matter
use_when: Obstacles prolong a pursuit without changing its methods, possibilities, or costs.
A character succeeds automatically despite the passage needing meaningful difficulty.
Repeated setbacks become interchangeable and the sequence grows without developing its concern.
mechanisms: Connecting the constraint to the particular want and its significance
Developing responses to an existing difficulty rather than continually adding unrelated barriers
Allowing competing legitimate purposes and outcomes that carry a cost even when successful
not_ideal_when: A cooperative or observational passage serves its purpose without frustrating a want.
Difficulty would require inventing a real constraint or treating another person’s boundary as something persistence must defeat.
example_user_queries: My character hits obstacle after obstacle but the story does not develop.
Success comes too easily in this scene.
How can an ordinary practical problem matter without making the danger bigger?
The person refusing my protagonist seems to exist only to create trouble.
My middle is getting longer because I keep adding new barriers.
How can succeeding still carry a meaningful cost?
The character keeps repeating the same failed attempt.
Can two people want the same outcome but disagree about how to reach it?
How can a refusal remain consequential without the protagonist overcoming it?
How do I preserve real constraints in nonfiction instead of inventing a tidier obstacle?

sources.title: 18.13: Finding the Core Conflict
sources.inspected_material: The official-page transcript on investment in participants, emotional reasons, and conflict between legitimate purposes or methods.
sources.supports: Connecting resistance to what matters to the participants rather than supplying opposition for its own sake.
sources.limits: No source example, exercise, numerical claim about horror novels, historical claim, or book recommendation is adopted. Rina and Mika are original fiction; access, boundaries, and nonfiction applications are editorial development.

articles.title: Make Events Cause Events
use_when: A synopsis lists engaging incidents but cannot show why they belong in this sequence.
Scenes could change places without changing later conditions.
A fresh problem arrives independently whenever the previous one ends.
goals: Distinctions between causal order and presentation order
mechanisms: Showing the practical conditions, knowledge, or options an earlier event changes
Grounding later responses in people’s purposes and circumstances without making them inevitable
Separating a supported causal relationship from succession, connective wording, or thematic association
not_ideal_when: An associative, observational, or thematic structure supplies the intended connection between incidents.
Evidence supports only succession or a qualified explanation in factual narrative.
example_user_queries: My synopsis is a series of and-then incidents.
Individual scenes are interesting but the story feels assembled from separate pieces.
How can one decision change what becomes possible later?
I added because and therefore but the plot still feels disconnected.
My characters seem to trigger the next event like parts of a machine.
Can I reveal a consequence before showing the event that produced it?
Can coincidence begin a story without controlling all of its later developments?
How do I distinguish a final trigger from a longer preparation for an event?
Does every memoir chapter need a continuous causal chain?
Two real events happened in order, but I cannot establish that one caused the other.

articles.title: Reveal Character Through Choice
use_when: Character labels never become consequential conduct.
A stated inner conflict does not affect what the person chooses.
A decision seems designed only to deliver a plot event despite established characterization.
mechanisms: Establishing available alternatives, relevant knowledge, and the costs of choosing
Showing how both the decision and its handling specify priorities
Distinguishing an interpretation of situated conduct from a permanent or complete character verdict
not_ideal_when: The person has little freedom or information and the narration would misrepresent their available alternatives.
A single observed act is being used to establish a real person’s enduring trait or hidden motive.
example_user_queries: I call my character loyal or ambitious but never show what those qualities mean.
The character says they are conflicted but acts as if only one concern exists.
How can a choice between two worthwhile options reveal a priority?
My character ignores an obvious alternative because I need a dramatic decision.
The outcome is the same, but can the way a person handles it change the characterization?
How do I make a surprising decision feel consistent with the person I have established?
Can regret remain after a character makes a defensible choice?
Does one small request for help prove a character has changed?
How can different viewpoints interpret the same decision differently?
What can I responsibly infer about a real person from one consequential action?

sources.inspected_material: The essay on believable character-driven decisions, meaningful alternatives, and the characterization cost of implausible behaviour used to prolong a plot.
sources.supports: Using decisions to characterize while preserving the person’s established competence and purposes.
sources.limits: No source police example, legal or clinical claim, exercise, or assertion that every person must be smart is adopted. Iris, Malik, and Ed are original fiction. Contextual interpretation, restricted options, and nonfiction limits are editorial development.

articles.title: Manage the Reader's Questions
use_when: Withheld context creates confusion rather than an uncertainty readers can follow.
Explanations arrive before the reader has a reason to want them.
Revelations supply surprises without developing an important question.
mechanisms: Supplying context that makes the unanswered question recognizable and significant
Changing the distribution of reader and character knowledge
Letting answers affect the situation before replacing them with further uncertainties
not_ideal_when: The reader needs an immediate answer to complete a practical task.
Withholding would conceal essential orientation, contradict the chosen viewpoint, or invent a secret in factual narrative.
example_user_queries: Readers say my opening is confusing rather than intriguing.
How much information can I withhold before the question stops making sense?
I reveal everything early and nothing makes readers want to continue.
Can telling the reader more make a scene more suspenseful?
How do I let readers know something a character does not?
My viewpoint character knows the answer but the narration keeps calling it the news.
Every revelation turns into another secret and nothing feels resolved.
How do I distinguish an open ending from an unanswered promise?
Can a quiet uncertainty sustain a scene without physical danger?
When should explanatory writing answer immediately instead of delaying information?

sources.author: Angela Ackerman
sources.title: Want to Build Tension? Encourage the Reader to Ask Questions
sources.inspected_material: The guest article’s discussion of anticipation, reader questions, and answering some questions as an exchange develops.
sources.supports: Using changing knowledge to support anticipation and giving answers a role in the passage.
sources.limits: No source dating example, exercise, required escalation, or universal reader response is adopted. Sera, Eno, and the mail-boat island are original fiction. Viewpoint, explanatory writing, and nonfiction qualifications are editorial development.

sources.supports: Recognizing that revealing information can create anticipation rather than simply reduce interest.
sources.limits: No source book example, duration limit on curiosity, marking exercise, or linked podcast/book review is adopted. The island alternatives, dramatic-irony arrangement, and reader-orientation comparisons are original editorial development.

articles.title: Let the Scene Change Something
use_when: A scene has activity but the next passage proceeds as if it never happened.
A scene repeats a condition without changing or establishing anything the work uses.
A consequential moment is present but obscured by surrounding material.
mechanisms: Comparing knowledge, options, relationships, expectations, or understanding before and after the encounter
Locating the turn that makes a difference available to the reader
Allowing character change, reader-only recognition, reflection, or purposeful stability according to the scene’s job
not_ideal_when: A scene deliberately establishes rest, routine, or continuity and an imposed revelation would distort it.
A factual account cannot establish the inner realization or decisive gesture the writer would like to give it.
example_user_queries: My scene is lively but the story is in the same place afterward.
Could I remove this encounter without changing what readers carry forward?
I know a significant moment is here but cannot find the turn.
Does every scene have to reverse the character’s fortune?
Can one person change their understanding while the other remains certain?
Can repetition reveal something new to the reader rather than change a character?
How do I show a consequence instead of saying things would never be the same?
What happens when later scenes ignore the decision made here?
Can a quiet or observational scene still develop a story?
How do I avoid inventing an instantaneous realization in memoir or reported narrative?
